description: You have to larp in order to find who you are.
summary:
Every autumn, a farmer asks one question: what should I plant next on this field? In Algeria and many developing regions there are no soil-lab records to answer it, so the same crop returns year after year, draining nitrogen, water and income.

Field Shift gives that farmer a clear answer in three seconds. Tap your field on a map and read: "Next year, sow lentil", with a score out of 100 and three reasons in plain words. A crop that the local rain or temperature cannot support is never proposed, and the farmer always keeps the final decision.

Behind the answer, NASA data replaces the missing lab: ten years of NASA POWER climate, MODIS, GPM, GLDAS and SRTM, combined with Sentinel 2, SoilGrids and two low-cost ESP32 stations in the field. Everything runs on an Android phone, in French and English.

On our pilot field in Sétif, Algeria, wheat every year scores 17.9; wheat, lentil, rapeseed scores 76.4: nitrogen back in the soil, less water stress and a crop that sells. In a country that imports three quarters of its wheat, better rotations protect soils, water and food security. Same land, better order.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Every autumn a farmer asks the same question: what do I plant next year on this field? Field Shift answers it in three seconds. The farmer taps the field on a map and reads: "Next year, sow lentil. Good plan, 76 out of 100. If you keep durum wheat every year: 18 out of 100." Below the answer come three reasons in plain words and one thing to watch. Curious users can open three deeper layers: the full calculation line by line, the local climate and live station readings, and sliders that change the weight of water, income and soil to see whether the rule changes its mind.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data. For each field the server downloads ten years of daily NASA POWER climate (rain, temperature, humidity, radiation, soil wetness), MODIS vegetation index and land surface temperature (ORNL DAAC web service), GPM IMERG monthly rain and GLDAS soil moisture and evaporation (GES DISC OPeNDAP), SRTM terrain (LP DAAC), Sentinel 2 vegetation at 10 m (Microsoft Planetary Computer) and SoilGrids soil properties (ISRIC). Our two ESP32 camera stations measure the field itself every minute: air temperature and humidity, light, an estimate of wind from sound, water, and photos.

2. Data fusion, at the data level, by cross-calibration (least squares). MODIS (250 m, since 2000) is rescaled on Sentinel 2 (10 m, since 2017) on matching dates: a long series with field-scale precision. NASA POWER (about 50 km) is rescaled on our station on common days, and the error before and after correction is shown. Rain from NASA POWER, GPM and the station is compared month by month.

3. The scoring rule. Score(B after A) = 50 + sum of coefficient × value, kept between 0 and 100. Nineteen criteria in three rotations, in this order: crops (same crop, same family, family back too soon, new family, market, forage, frost, heat), water (water deficit against FAO 56 crop needs, two thirsty crops in a row, recharge, drought tolerance, deep roots) and soil (nitrogen fixation, nitrogen demand, months of bare soil, legume cover crop, organic matter, fallow rest). A cover crop is inserted when three or more bare months follow each other. Values are 0 or 1, a 1 to 5 rating divided by 5, a share between 0 and 1, or a number of months, so anyone can redo the calculation by hand. Example: lentil after durum wheat = 50 + 15 (nitrogen) + 9.6 (market) + 8 (new family) + 8 (water recharge) + 4.8 + 3.2 + 2.4 − 3.75 (bare months) − 6.06 (frost) = 91.2.

4. Realism checks. A weighted sum always names a winner, even where nothing grows, so three ruling-out criteria apply before any score: a crop is excluded if rain and irrigation cover less than 35% of its water needs, or if its cycle has more frost days or days above 35 °C than it can take. A point at sea is refused using a 5 km land mask (NOAA GLOBE). If no crop is viable, the app says so and suggests irrigation instead of recommending a crop bound to fail.

5. The rotation is built greedily, one year at a time; the last year also scores the return to the first crop, and the rotation score is the cyclic mean. Three farmer profiles (potato grower, cereal grower, livestock farmer) change only the first crop, irrigation and two coefficients.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Rotations that bring a legume after cereals give nitrogen back to the soil, break disease cycles and save water. On our pilot field the rule moves a wheat monoculture from 17.9 to 76.4, and a potato grower from 39.3 to 82.9. The rule is not tied to one country: the same coefficients run on any point of the northern hemisphere, from the Algerian high plains to Kansas and Punjab, with ten years of NASA climate downloaded once and cached.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND HARDWARE

Python (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, pandas, NumPy), MariaDB / MySQL (31 tables, 8 views, 4 triggers, 3 stored procedures, 34 foreign keys; a trigger flags impossible readings before they are written), Vue 3, Vite, Leaflet and Chart.js, French and English interface, 52 automated tests. Hardware: Freenove ESP32 WROVER CAM and ESP32 S3 CAM boards, DHT11, photoresistor, KY-038 microphone, analog water sensor, programmed in Arduino C++. Server: an Android phone running Termux, which the stations reach over Wi-Fi.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The whole system fits in a pocket: the farmer's own phone is the server. The interface follows a map app: the answer first, details only for those who want them, and a small reward (a leaf lights up) for each layer of detail discovered. And the decision rule is fully transparent: no black box, every point can be traced.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Four disciplines worked together: computer science (site, database, server), agronomy (crop catalogue and coefficients), physics (climate, satellites, data fusion) and robotics (field station). Known limits, stated openly: nitrogen is estimated, not measured; coefficients are expert choices not yet calibrated on local yields; the station correction is computed and shown but does not yet enter the score; the southern hemisphere is not supported yet. The tool suggests; the farmer decides.
